title: What shall we do? (Luke 3:1–14)
hookLine: John tells the crowds: share your coat, don't cheat, don't extort

lines: THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE WILDERNESS.
cards: Luke opens this chapter like a news anchor reading the date. The fifteenth year of the emperor Tiberius. Pontius Pilate governing Judea.
Herod ruling Galilee. His brother Philip, another ruler named Lysanias, the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Seven powerful names, the people with palaces and armies and seals.
Then the sentence lands somewhere else entirely: "the word of God came unto John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness." Not to the emperor. Not to the palace.
To the son of an old priest, out in the empty country by the Jordan. And the crowds start walking out to hear him.

teach.b: John doesn't flatter them: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come?" Don't lean on your family tree, he says; the axe is already at the root of the trees.
"Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance." Repentance: a turn in how you live. And the crowd asks the honest question: "What shall we do then?"
John doesn't tell them to move to the wilderness or give up their trades. His answers are almost ordinary.
To everyone: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise." The coat is the everyday tunic. If you have a spare, someone else is cold.
Tax collectors come to be baptized: "Master, what shall we do?"

teach.h: TAX COLLECTORS: NO MORE THAN APPOINTED.
teach.b: He doesn't tell them to quit: "Exact no more than that which is appointed you." Collect what's owed. Don't pad the bill.

teach.h: SOLDIERS: NO VIOLENCE, NO FALSE ACCUSING.
teach.b: Then soldiers, men with weapons and power over civilians: "And what shall we do?"

"Do violence to no man, neither accuse any falsely; and be content with your wages." Three groups, three answers, each fitting the person's actual job. In Luke, turning around doesn't start in a temple or a monastery.
It starts at the closet, the tax booth and the checkpoint: at your own counter, with your own receipts.

how: In the Revised Common Lectionary, John's preaching from Luke 3 is read in Advent, and some Christian charities point to Luke 3:11 for coat drives and clothing closets.

o: a heavy outer cloak worn only by the rich
the robe a priest wore to burn incense
the everyday tunic, the coat John says to share

games.q: who asked, and what did John answer? tap the pairs.
p: laid unto the root of the trees

s: John told the tax collectors to quit their jobs
he told them to collect no more than was appointed.
Luke dates John's preaching to the fifteenth year of Tiberius
Luke lists the emperor, governors and high priests first.
John told the crowds to live in the desert like him
his answers were ordinary: share clothes and food.

games.q: you're a soldier standing in the crowd at the Jordan. you ask John what you should do. what does he say?
o: lay down your weapons and leave the army.
no violence, no false accusations, be content with your wages.
come and live in the wilderness with me.
games.why: John answers each group in its own job: don't bully, don't lie about people, don't squeeze extra out of them.

practice: Ask John's question about your own week: what shall I do?

Walk through the places where money or time changes hands, a bill, a tip, hours logged, a price you set, a favor never paid back, and let one small place come up where you could be a little more honest or more generous than you need to be.
Don't make it dramatic; John didn't. If you pray, ask the crowd's question and listen; if not, simply name that one place.

wordCard.voice: Chiton, the Greek word for tunic, the garment worn next to the skin: the coat John tells the crowd to share, alongside his plain answers for tax collectors and soldiers too.

orig.note: Greek: a tunic, the garment worn next to the skin. the "coat" in Luke 3:11.

carryVoice: Your line: share your coat. Small, fair and ordinary: that's where the turn begins. Day five hundred thirteen.
